A1.text:
From the UK to the Gulf, are US overseas bases becoming liabilities?
For decades, these bases allowed the US to wage faraway wars and protect allies. Now, Iran has changed that calculation — for friends hosting these facilities, and for Washington.
Doha, Qatar — Late one morning in March 1999, a United States B-52 bomber took off from RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, headed southeast. Seven more jets followed, at two-minute intervals.
It was the start of the US-led NATO bombing of Yugoslavia, a campaign in which the Fairford base served as both a pivotal launchpad for American jets and as a fuel station for fighter planes. The British base had served a similar role during the Gulf War in 1991, and would do so again during the 2003 Iraq war and in the early stages of the US-Israeli war on Iran that began on February 28, 2026.
But in October, the US pulled all 12 of its B-1 Lancer bombers from the Gloucestershire base, amid fears that they were no longer safe there from a growing Iranian threat. Days earlier, British security forces had made several arrests, and the country’s government has accused Iran of being behind a plot to target the base — a charge Tehran has denied.
RAF Fairford is not alone. Earlier this month, the US withdrew a dozen planes from another British base, RAF Mildenhall. And in July, reports said that the US had relocated many of its military assets from its bases in the Gulf that were badly hit by Iran during the war, instead moving them to bases in Jordan, while also considering a proposal to shift them to Israel.
For decades, these bases have served as the sharp edge of the US military’s ability to project power and wage wars thousands of miles from home. For close allies, whether in Europe or the Gulf, they also worked as security guarantors against other threats.
But Iran’s ability to severely damage US facilities in the Middle East during the war, and pose a threat as far as the UK, has for the first time turned these critical strategic assets into potential liabilities, both for American allies and for the US itself, say analysts.
“The US security umbrella is becoming a double-edged sword,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. “When the security of US bases is called into question, it changes Washington’s calculation of their strategic benefits. It also gives European and Gulf states reason to think seriously about the bases, given that they are becoming targets.”
How the Iran war changed the bargain
Hosting American bases has long been perceived as integral to how US allies, whether in Europe, the Gulf or East Asia, deter threats that they themselves face.
Former US President Barack Obama once spoke of an “ironclad commitment” to Gulf security, while Britain regularly invokes its so-called “special relationship” with the United States. In doing so, Britain and the Gulf have long cast themselves as willing partners to a power that — at least before current President Donald Trump — presented itself as the benevolent guarantor of its allies’ security.
But a spate of recent security incidents, many linked to the war on Iran, is testing that narrative and raising questions about whose interests these commitments serve, and whether hosting American forces could be bringing danger closer to home.
US prosecutors have charged three men they describe as Iranian-backed operatives over their alleged roles in plotting nearly 20 attacks across the United States and Europe, including on RAF Fairford.
Meanwhile, in the Gulf, Iran explicitly cited the presence of US bases as justification for targeting its neighbours, bombing Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain and Kuwait. Iran also bombed Oman, which does not have a permanent US base; and Jordan and Iraq, beyond the Gulf, which do host major US military facilities.

Huang's potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly $4 trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of AI chips at the center of the global artificial-intelligence boom and US-China technology rivalry.
Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia's stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.
"Huang being removed immediately could be challenging for Nvidia since it does not have a succession plan in place ... If Mr. Huang broke the law or violated company policies, the board is likely to act as soon as they have proof," Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, said.
The company's shares slid about 8% in after-hours trading after the Wall Street Journal first reported that Nvidia was preparing to oust Huang. Including Wednesday's after-hours selloff, Nvidia has lost about $600 billion in stock market value this week since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a Chinese businesswoman.
Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.
The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.
When reached by phone Wednesday and asked about his relationship with Ms. Powell, Mr. Huang said, "I don't think you should be talking to me directly." He then hung up, the New York Times reported.
Nvidia and Powell did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not immediately verify the report.
LEADERSHIP UNCERTAINTY
The reports mark a sharp escalation in a controversy that began with revelations about Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence has said was involved in facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms.
US stock futures sank, with Nasdaq futures NQc1 down 1%. However, shares of rival chipmakers AMD AMD.O and Broadcom AVGO.O rose 4% and 3%, respectively, in after-hours trading, which an analyst said reflected the view that those chip producers would pick up market share.
Investors and analysts said while demand for Nvidia's chips would be unlikely to drop in the near term, the broader universe of companies backed by the company might suffer.
"Nvidia is also at the centre of the circular financing which is providing capital to the investment boom," said Nick Ferres, chief investment officer at Vantage Point Asset Management in Singapore.
"They are financing their customers. In these types of booms or bubbles, sometimes all it takes is a slowdown to shift it into the bust phase."
In a memo to employees on Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and took "full responsibility," but gave no details about the relationship.
The same day, Nvidia's board launched an investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. The probe is being overseen by independent directors with outside legal counsel. At the time, the board expressed confidence in Huang.
US President Donald Trump has said he had not discussed the allegations with Huang but voiced support for the Nvidia chief, calling him "an honorable guy" who had "done an amazing job for our country."
Huang faces a potential congressional subpoena if he doesn't respond to a request to provide a closed-door briefing about the allegations that he had a close relationship with the Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing.
Separately, Axios reported on Wednesday, citing high-level sources, that US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick stalled President Donald Trump's crackdown on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's chips to China.

A11.text:
Indonesia vice president resigns amid dispute over eligibility
Gibran Rakabuming Raka, son of former President Joko Widodo, resigns as court questions his overseas education credentials.
Indonesia’s vice president has resigned in the midst of a scandal over his high school diploma, adding pressure on a government facing widespread dissatisfaction over the economy, corruption and wildfires.
Gibran Rakabuming Raka submitted his resignation to President Prabowo Subianto and parliament on Thursday, the speaker of the People’s Consultative Assembly told reporters.
Speaking hours later at a press conference alongside Gibran at the Presidential Palace, Prabowo said he had accepted the resignation with a “heavy heart”.
Gibran is the eldest son of former President Joko Widodo, Prabowo’s immediate predecessor.
“There will always be political dynamics in public office, that’s normal,” Widodo told reporters from his hometown in Solo after the resignation, adding that he had reminded his son that political positions are temporary.
“We will continue to support President Prabowo’s government, especially programmes that serve the interests of the broader public,” the former leader said.
Gibran, 39, leaves office after serving two years of his five-year term as questions grew over his eligibility after recent court rulings disputed his educational credentials.
Under Indonesia’s Constitution, a vice presidential vacancy does not trigger a new election. The office remains vacant until the People’s Consultative Assembly elects a replacement from two candidates nominated by the president within 60 days.
Gibran had offered to resign on Tuesday during a meeting with the president, saying he wanted to avoid a prolonged political controversy.
But a cabinet minister said Prabowo urged Gibran at the time to defend himself, and it wasn’t clear whether he had accepted the resignation offer.
Indonesia’s vice president does not have many constitutionally defined powers apart from acting as the president’s representative at official events and taking over if his boss is incapacitated.
The Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court ruled last month that the documents Gibran submitted regarding his overseas education did not meet election requirements. His critics have accused him of never receiving a high school diploma.
A subsequent petition submitted on Wednesday to the leaders of the House of Representatives by 120 lawmakers from eight political parties began a parliamentary process that could lead to Gibran’s impeachment.
Under Indonesian law, House leaders must establish a special committee to examine whether Gibran has violated the constitution by serving as vice president despite allegedly failing to meet election requirements.
If lawmakers determine there is sufficient basis for the accusation, the House must ask the Constitutional Court to rule on whether a constitutional violation has occurred.
Gibran’s downfall comes as thousands of protesters have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest economic hardship, corruption, perceived authoritarianism and the government’s handling of months of devastating wildfires emitting a toxic haze that has made thousands of people ill.
It also comes amid investigations into allegations that top police officials were involved in wiretapping targeting the president. The academic credentials investigation was apparently not related to the wiretapping scandal.

Angaben des Außenministeriums Russischer Botschafter in den USA ist tot
Russlands Botschafter in den USA, Alexander Dartschijew, ist nach Angaben der Regierung in Moskau im Alter von 66 Jahren gestorben. Der Diplomat sei »plötzlich« gestorben, teilte das russische Außenministerium am Mittwoch mit, ohne weitere Angaben zur Todesursache zu machen. Das Ministerium würdigte Dartschijew als »herausragenden Diplomaten« und »brillanten USA-Experten«.
Das US-Außenministerium teilte seinerseits mit, dass Dartschijew am Mittwoch in Moskau verstorben sei. Es sprach der Familie und den Angehörigen sein Beileid aus. Für weitere Einzelheiten zu seinem Tod verwies ein Ministeriumssprecher an die russische Regierung.
Moskau warnt vor »unnötigen Verschwörungstheorien«
Ministeriumssprecherin Marija Sacharowa schrieb später auf Telegram, Dartschijew sei in Moskau an den Folgen einer chronischen Erkrankung gestorben. Sie warnte, Medien sollten wegen seines Todes nicht in »unnötige Verschwörungstheorien« verfallen. In der Vergangenheit hatten plötzliche Todesfälle in der russischen Elite oder von in Ungnade gefallenen Personen immer wieder zu Spekulationen und internationaler Aufmerksamkeit geführt. Mehrere Regierungsvertreter und hochrangige Wirtschaftsleute starben etwa nach Stürzen aus dem Fenster.
Dartschijew hatte den Botschafterposten in Washington im März 2025 angetreten, rund zwei Monate nach der Rückkehr von US-Präsident Donald Trump ins Weiße Haus. Aufgrund der Spannungen zwischen Moskau und der Regierung von Trumps Vorgänger Joe Biden im Kontext der russischen Offensive in der Ukraine war der Posten des russischen Botschafters in den USA ab Oktober 2024 nicht mehr besetzt gewesen.

A146.text:
Tundu Lissu verdict: What does it mean for Tanzania's democracy?
November 11, 2026
On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections.
The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty.
Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure and rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025.
Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.
Tanzania's most dramatic trial in decades
Few opposition figures have shaped modern Tanzanian politics as dramatically as Lissu. A lawyer by training and one of the country's most outspoken critics of the ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), Lissu has spent years challenging the political establishment.
Over the years, he has been repeatedly arrested and detained. In 2017, he survived an attempt on his life by unknown gunmen outside his residence in the capital Dodoma, sustaining multiple bullet wounds.
His trial in the run-up to the October 2025 general election continued to keep him and the opposition in the public eye following his arrest in April that same year in the southwestern town of Mbinga.
Why was Tundu Lissu arrested?
Prosecuters accused Lissu of encouraging the public to prevent the 2025 election from taking place and charged him with one count of treason.
As legal evidence, they cited social media posts he had made, in which he was seen to be calling on Tanzanians to boycott the vote over concerns about possible electoral malpractice.
In the end, the election went ahead without Chadema on October 29. It was marred by violence on an unprecedented in scale in Tanzania, with security forces even firing live ammunition at protesters.
Francis Ibrahim, an independent political analyst based in Dar es Salaam, told DW that "heads have to roll from the law enforcement side who overstretched their mandate, all the way to the people who financed, planned and organized [this crackdown]."
Following the election violence and a nationwide internet shutdown and curfew, incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan was named winner with 98% of the vote.
What does the verdict mean for democracy?
Ibrahim believes that the removal of the capital treason charge could be interpreted as a move towards rapprochment with voters.
"What I can tell you is that they are looking for a political deescalation that could solve the crisis," he explained, adding that Lissu might yet get to have a small say in politics after all.
"There has to be a process of [creating] a new constitution, and it needs everybody on the table," he said, adding that Lissu might therefore perhaps be released early in order to partake in discussions and negotiations.
But in late July, when President Suluhu Hassan met with representatives of more than a dozen political parties to discuss national reconciliation and constitutional reform, Chadema officials were explicitly not party to the consultations.
Politics at play behind the verdict?
Public opinion meanwhile varies on Lissu's verdict, with many Tanzanians saying that the trial was politically motivated in their view.
Ruqaya Mohammed, the National Deputy Secretary of the oppsition ACT-Wazalendo party's youth wing, told DW, "we are getting into a darker space in our political arena."
"I think it's the right time now, as a nation, to have open dialogue on some reforms, on the legal perspective and electoral reforms. Maybe if we manage ... that, we can see a light," she added.
Most others, however, remain reluctant to go on record for fear of reprisal. A musician and human rights advocate was among few who agreed to speak to DW — on the strict condition of anonymity.

A17.text:
Fighting intensifies in Yemen as Houthis deny targeting Mecca
World Health Organisation says more 320,000 people have been displaced in Yemen fighting since August 1.
Yemen’s Houthis have rejected Saudi claims that they targeted Islam’s holiest city, Mecca, as casualties surge in the war between the internationally recognised government and the Iran-allied Houthis.
A Houthi spokesperson on Wednesday denied what he called Saudi “lies” that the Iran-allied group had launched a drone towards Mecca, saying instead that a drone was launched at a pumping station in Yanbu on the Red Sea, and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport was targeted with three cruise missiles.
Earlier, Saudi-led coalition forces said they had intercepted three cruise missiles launched towards Riyadh, along with drones launched towards Mecca and Saudi Arabia’s southern regions.
Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence Authority said debris from the interception of two ballistic missiles fell in the village of Sabuhah in Mecca province.
“This hostile targeting of civilian objects constitutes a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and reflects the dangerous hostile approach pursued by the Houthi militia,” Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said early on Thursday.
Attacks on Aden
Suspected Houthi missile strikes in the kingdom came as fighting intensified inside Yemen between the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of the internationally recognised government and Houthi fighters.
At least 138 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded in hundreds of targeted attacks, according to Majed Abdullah al-Nuzaili, the spokesperson for Yemen’s army.
In a post on X, al-Nuzaili said Yemen’s Saudi-backed army had carried out 773 field artillery attacks on top of 44 drone strikes and 37 rocket attacks in al-Jawf, Marib, al-Bayda and Taiz governorates.
He also said Saudi-led coalition forces had conducted 23 air strikes against the Houthis, damaging 86 heavy weapons and military vehicles.
Despite their successes on the field on various fronts, the Saudi-backed forces have failed to stop Houthi attacks on the al-Buraiqa district in Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
“The repeated shelling by the terrorist Houthi militia on the city of Aden, most recently targeting the densely populated al-Buraiqa district, reflects the militia’s established pattern of targeting civilians and terrorising innocent people,” Minister of Information Salem al-Awalqi said in a social media post.
“These assaults will fail to break the will of the people of Aden or undermine their resilience; rather, they will only strengthen their resolve to confront the aggression and defend their city,” he added.
Yemen’s Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said his forces had “successfully targeted” a Saudi coalition military command and control centre in Aden’s al-Buraiqa district with “several ballistic missiles”.
In a Telegram post, Saree said the facility was responsible for directing and overseeing Saudi military reinforcements across active fronts in Lahij, al-Dhale, Taiz and other governorates.
Rising casualties
Casualties from the fighting in Yemen have risen sharply to 11,755, including 2,098 killed and 9,657 wounded, as of November 8, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The United Nations agency said that more than 2,000 casualties were recorded in just nine days, with Marib and Lahij among the worst affected governorates.
More than 320,000 people have been displaced as a result of fighting since August 1, including almost 16,000 forced to flee their homes in the past week, it said.
The WHO said strikes have also hit health facilities and ambulances, and warned that critical fuel shortages are disrupting emergency medical services in Taiz.
Despite the delivery of medical supplies and a vaccination campaign targeting nearly one million children, major gaps remain in trauma care, rehabilitation, and mental health services, it said.

A180.text:
New restrictions to Starshield network 'kill more Ukrainians', Zelensky says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday said that Ukrainian military units had recorded new and significant disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service in recent days, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Thursday that Ukraine's military faced new "systematic" restrictions to Starshield satellite internet, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX service which plays a key role for frontline communications.
Ukraine first reported problems using Starshield last month following a row between Zelensky and US President Donald Trump over a US-Russia diesel deal. Zelensky said the latest issues were not "random errors".
Trump and Musk denied responsibility for the last outages, although Musk later accused Ukraine of misusing SpaceX's Starlink internet service for military purposes before all sides said full access had been restored.
Starshield is the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink.
"Our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now," Zelensky said on social media.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
"Systematic speed restrictions are being imposed," Zelensky said, adding they were "not random errors".
"This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes," he added.
Starshield systems were not working above 100 miles per hour (161 kilometres per hour), Zelensky said.
The speed limits were proving a "significant complication in intercepting Russian jet-powered drones", which move much faster than that.
The apparent restrictions come as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner meet Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow following two days of talks in Abu Dhabi searching for a deal to end the almost five-year war.

A2.text:
US envoys arrive in Moscow for Russia-Ukraine talks with Putin
The meeting with Kushner and Witkoff comes after two days of trilateral talks in the UAE yielded no breakthrough.
United States envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in their latest push for a peace deal in Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s special envoy, met Kushner and Witkoff at their plane on Thursday morning and accompanied them to central Moscow.
The meeting comes on the heels of two days of trilateral peace talks in the United Arab Emirates that concluded in the capital, Abu Dhabi, on Wednesday with news of another planned major prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the nearly five-year war.
The US said differences remained on major issues, including territory, but some progress had been made on post-war security guarantees.
Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin’s demands to surrender all of its eastern region of Donbas in return for peace.
The Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US in nine months.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said one of the goals of Thursday’s visit would be for the US team to persuade Putin to invite Europeans to the negotiation process.
“Ukraine and the US want the European partners to be involved while Moscow is adamant about talks without the Europeans, and that’s why they’ve been largely excluded from the process,” she said.
Shapovalova added that the US delegation would bring Putin an updated proposal for a peace plan and the presence of Dmitriev in the talks was an indication that they would address some of the more complex issues.
European leaders meet in Dublin
During the US-backed effort to revive talks, leaders from more than 40 European countries gathered in Dublin on Thursday for a summit focused on the continent’s security.
The meeting of the European Political Community (EPC) brought together heads of state and government from the European Union and other European countries, including the United Kingdom. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also attended.
The EPC was established in 2022 as a forum for countries both inside and outside the 27-nation EU.
Zelenskyy and his European allies are expected to discuss this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi.
Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, and Witkoff are scheduled to meet Zelenskyy in Dublin on Friday after talking to Putin.
Audrey Macalpine, reporting from Kyiv, said Ukrainians do not believe the talks in Moscow will yield results. “Over the past two days, we saw just another prisoner exchange, which has been the case in previous talks,” the correspondent said.
“When it comes to the negotiations, not much has changed in terms of where these two sides stand,” Macalpine added. “Perhaps the biggest thing of note [in the talks] was that they took place at all.”
Meanwhile, French Minister Delegate for European Affairs Benjamin Haddad on Thursday said the EU will approve more sanctions against Russia.
“On Monday, we will take new sanctions against Russia on 150 additional entities, 50 banks, and it’s France which proposed the bulk of the entities to add,” Haddad told LCI television.

A26.text:
Israeli strike on southern Gaza hospital kills six, Gaza civil defence says
CAIRO, Nov 12 (Reuters) - An Israeli airstrike on a building at Nasser Hospitalinsouthern Gaza killed at least six people, including a surgeon, and wounded 20 others early on Thursday, a spokesman for Gaza's civil defence service told Reuters.
The Israeli military later said it had targeted a senior Hamas militant and other members of the group's armed wing who it said were operating inside the hospital in Khan Younis.
In a statement, the military accused Hamas of using the hospital complex as a command centre for military operations, including storing weapons, operating command-and-control rooms and using hospital facilities as observation posts and shelters for fighters.
Reuters could not independently verify the Israeli military's allegations.
Mahmoud Basal, the spokesperson for Gaza's civildefence, said the Israeli airstrike hit the surgery department of the hospital, causing extensive damage.
Medics identified the dead surgeon as Rezik Abushira.
Reuters video from inside the hospital showed extensive damage, with rubble and furniture strewn across rooms and wires dangling from damaged ceilings.
People carried injured patients on stretchers through debris-covered corridors, while others helped the wounded walk through the wreckage. Several bodies were also seen being carried away as firefighters worked outside.
A Hamas spokesperson condemned the strike as a "fully-fledged war crime".
Israel, which has stepped up its attacks on the enclave, says Hamas is trying to regroup and rebuild its arsenal.Hamas says it is committed to a year-old ceasefire and accuses Israel of trying to undermine the agreement.
At least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since the deal was agreed, according to the territory's health officials, while Israel says four soldiers have been killed.
Gaza health authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed since Israel began its assault on Gaza in October 2023. Israel launched its offensive after Hamas gunmen led an attack on southern Israel in which it says about 1,200 people were killed.
(Reporting by Nidal Al-Mughrabi, Hatem Maher and Jana Choukeir; Editing by Cynthia Osterman and Kate Mayberry)

Motor racing-Hamilton urges Israel to let Gaza aid in after Rafah visit
Nov 11 (Reuters) - Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.
Hamilton, a seven-times world champion, arrived in El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent's aid warehouses.
"The past three years of Israel's genocide in Gaza is appalling. It's an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less," the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were regularly held up or faced major delays.
He said that at a nearby logistics centre, items had been rejected for "crazy reasons", including sleeping bags, first-aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs, and footballs for children.
"Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. No excuse," he said."I don't want us to get used to their suffering. I don't want us to look away."
Hamilton, 41, is an advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded Mission 44, a charity that supports young people and works to improve their access to education and employment.
He is fourth in the drivers' championship. Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races remaining.
(Reporting by Angelica Medina in Mexico City; Editing by Sonali Paul)

DUBAI, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles and drones launched towards Riyadh, Mecca and other regions on Wednesday, as hostilities between the Iran-aligned group and the kingdom worsen.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Yemeni group said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles headed to the Riyadh region, two drones aimed at Mecca and southern areas and two missiles pointed towards the west.
Mecca, home to sites sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam's holiest city and the focal point of the annual hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims undertake each year.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree later denied targeting Mecca with a drone, saying the group's operations target oil facilities and military bases.
Saree also said the Houthis had attacked a pumping station in Saudi Arabia's Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the blocked Strait of Hormuz. There was no Saudi confirmation of the Houthi statement.
Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in the cities of Taif, Yanbu and Khamis Mushait later on Wednesday, then announced the danger had passed, state television reported.
The militia, which controls most of the populous parts of Yemen, has intensified attacks on the Saudi capital in recent days, saying it was responding to Saudi attacks in Yemen. A Houthi attack on Sunday damaged an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh's financial hub.
Wednesday's interceptions marked the second consecutive day that Saudi air defences had intercepted Houthi missiles launched towards Riyadh, after they downed a ballistic missile and a cruise missile on Tuesday, the coalition said.
Last month, a Houthi attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Renewed fighting between the two sides has intensified since September, when the Houthis advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis have since stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up airstrikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response.
(Reporting by Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir, Yomna Ehab and Ahmed TolbaEditing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Philippa Fletcher and Cynthia Osterman)

A3.text:
India bypasses own rules to buy Israeli phone-hacking tech
India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend far beyond just cloning phones to accessing cloud-based data from social media platforms like Instagram and Tinder.
New Delhi, India – India has exempted an Israeli phone-hacking company from New Delhi’s own rules, allowing it to sell phone-extraction products and surveillance technology to government agencies and sparking concerns and criticism from rights groups and activists.
An investigation by the digital-rights group Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) found Indian Home Minister Amit Shah, a close confidante of Prime Minister Narendra Modi, signed off on exemptions from “make in India” procurement rules, clearing the way for government forensic institutions to buy at least 422 items of foreign technology, including products made by the Israeli firm Cellebrite.
Modi’s federal government and state governments ruled by his Bharatiya Janata Party are not the only ones who bought this Israeli technology. States governed by the opposition Indian National Congress party, including Himachal Pradesh, Keralam and Karnataka, also purchased similar phone-extraction and cloning tools.
A review of documents revealed that India’s expansive surveillance capabilities extend far beyond just cloning phones and extracting data without passwords to accessing cloud-based data from social media platforms – such as Instagram, X and Tinder – as well as data from connected devices such as Amazon’s Alexa and Google Home.
Experts argued that India’s current laws offer no guardrails against overreaching surveillance and the data extractions happen in a legal grey zone.
“It is clear that there is an expansion of India’s surveillance capabilities and it is becoming both wider and deeper,” said Vrinda Bhandari, a lawyer in the Supreme Court who works on digital rights and privacy issues.
“It’s now easier to conduct mass surveillance rather than targeted, specific surveillance and also possible to do more intrusive surveillance,” she told Al Jazeera. “[Today,] surveillance gives you a richer picture of an individual’s life.”
From Instagram to Tinder: Extracting cloud-based data
The IFF reviewed a letter also seen by Al Jazeera from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs dated January 7 in which Shah signed off on a wide-ranging, one-year waiver of “make in India” rules to clear a path for buying at least 422 forensic items.
Under “make in India” procurement rules, preference must be given to eligible Indian manufacturers over foreign suppliers in awarding government contracts. However, the rules allow exemptions with the approval of the minister in charge of the procuring department.
Another letter by the ministry dated January 20 showed Shah permitted the National Investigation Agency (NIA) to buy Israeli company Cellebrite’s Premium Tool on a three-year licence for about 50 million rupees ($529,947).
In specifications demanded by the government that were revealed in a review of tender bids, “solution” software must be capable of using login tokens recovered from seized phones or computers to access more than 100 cloud services. Login tokens are in effect digital keys that keep users signed in to online accounts.
Although an exemption for a company does not confirm whether a certain product was purchased by any government agency, it points to the range of forensic capabilities that opened up for procurement by Indian agencies.
From the 422-item exemption list, the IFF identified 118 items under digital and multimedia forensics, including Israeli company Cellebrite’s Pathfinder, Inseyets On-Prem Pro and Inseyets Offline.
Cellebrite’s tools have been used against journalists and activists in countries like Serbia, Jordan, Kenya and Russia.

He added that Russia's buffer zone along its border with Ukraine was already substantial and would keep expanding, according to the Interfax news agency.

A35.text:
Yemen security sources report strikes on Aden
Yemeni security sources reported Houthi strikes on Wednesday in Aden, the seat of the country's internationally recognised government, saying they had targeted camps belonging to forces fighting the Iran-backed group.
Earlier in the day, in Yemen's Houthi-controlled capital Sanaa, crowds had gathered for the funeral of dozens of people killed last week in strikes blamed on Saudi Arabia, which also reported intercepting fresh attacks on Wednesday.
Yemen has been reeling from war since 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa, with a Saudi-led coalition entering the conflict a year later in support of the government.
In July, a fragile 2022 truce fell apart, and Saudi Arabia has since traded blows with the Houthis, who have struck Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites.
The two Yemeni security sources told AFP that two missiles had targeted a camp of the Saudi-led coalition in Aden's west on Wednesday.
They said a third projectile, which they later identified as a drone, targeted another camp belonging to Yemeni forces in the city's centre, adding that it was intercepted.
Aden was attacked several times last month by the Houthis, including on October 15, when they launched a deadly missile strike on the presidential palace in Aden that killed four people, according to government military sources.
The Saudi-led coalition on Wednesday said it had "intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area".
Riyadh has been repeatedly attacked since hostilities resumed, with its international airport forced to close for two weeks last month following deadly strikes.
On Sunday, the Houthis damaged a skyscraper in the capital's financial district belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco.
- Large crowds -
The Houthis said a Saudi strike on Saturday hit the village of al-Shariya, outside Sanaa, killing 44 people, including 21 children, and injuring 40 others.
The group's Almasirah television reported another strike as emergency personnel headed to the site to dig out survivors. AFP could not verify the claim.
Mourners prayed on Wednesday at Sanaa's Mosque of the People and chanted "Death to America! Death to Israel!" according to an AFP photographer present.
Men and boys in white and brown-olive robes, some bearing rifles and traditional daggers, stood by the coffins near the mosque. Draped in white cloth, the caskets bore the photographs and names of those killed.
The resumption in fighting has killed more than 1,600 people and displaced more than 300,000 in Yemen, according to the UN.
After prayers, the funeral procession took the bodies to al-Shariya for burial.
- 'Having a meal' -
Earlier this week, resident Daifallah Sarhan, a farmer, told AFP "they were all innocent... People were simply having a meal with their families and children" when the strikes hit.
The 2022 truce fell apart in July after the Houthis allowed an Iranian plane to land in the capital in defiance of Saudi control over Yemeni airspace, setting off a spate of attacks.
Later, the Houthis declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began hitting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before seizing Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning campaign.
The group has in turn reported frequent Saudi airstrikes.
Twenty-six people have been killed in Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia since hostilities resumed.

Nvidia’s board is set to decide the future of its founder Jensen Huang after revelations that he had a romantic relationship with a company executive, days after it emerged that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.
The board held urgent talks on Wednesday night after news broke of the Nvidia chief executive’s relationship with Kimberly Powell, the chipmaker’s vice-president of healthcare, according to people familiar with the matter.
The relationship with an Nvidia employee deepens an already damaging scandal for the $4.2 trillion semiconductor group. Huang on Sunday admitted to having an affair, two days after the FT reported his romantic links to an executive at an Nvidia client, who US officials believe is a Chinese intelligence asset.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Powell, who has worked at Nvidia for more than 18 years and is among its more prominent public figures, could not be reached for comment.
The board, which unusually has no chair in a testament to Huang’s singular role at Nvidia, this week hired a former federal prosecutor to investigate his affair with the suspected spy. But the board has thus far backed Huang to remain as chief executive.
The directors could opt to have Huang step back from his duties as CEO while the investigation proceeds and the board intensifies succession planning. Or they could now push for his immediate departure.
Nvidia’s annual reports and corporate governance paperwork have until now included no specific reference to “succession planning” and set out no details for how it would replace its CEO, even in an emergency.

A466.text:
Zelenskiy says Starshield speed limited again, hampering Ukraine's defences
Nov 12 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Thursday that Ukrainian military units had recorded significant disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications service for several days, affecting the entire front line and Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine.
In a post on Telegram, Zelenskiy said that systemic restrictions were limiting the speed at which Starshield could be used to 161 kph (100 mph). Starshield is the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications service.
As a result of the restrictions, Ukrainian interceptors could not reach sufficient speed to down Russian jet-powered drones, with some hits already occurring, Zelenskiy said.
"This helps Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes on Ukraine," Zelenskiy said. He added that Ukraine was trying to clarify the reasons for the restriction with the US side.
In mid-October, Ukrainian officials said SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and Starshield, cutting off drones and other equipment moving faster than about 160 kph (100 mph) amid tensions with the Trump administration over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on October 24.
The new disruptions come a day after the end of two days of peace talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, brokered by the United States, the first such meeting since February. A Ukrainian official said there was no mention of the disruptions during the talks and it was unclear who had made the decision.
Ukraine has carried out a series of strikes against Russian refineries and energy installations in recent weeks, as Moscow has continued to pummel Ukrainian electricity infrastructure and cities with drones and missiles. REUTERS

A469.text:
Nordic countries to work towards common defence deal, Norway says
OSLO, Nov 12 - The Nordic countries of Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Finland and Iceland will work towards establishing a common defence deal in order to boost NATO's overall ability to deter and defend, Norway's Defence Minister Tore Sandvik said on Thursday.
The nations are all NATO members since Finland and Sweden joined the military alliance in 2023 and 2024, and have worked since then to improve their cooperation, for instance by conducting joint military and civilian preparedness exercises.
"We have already come a long way within the framework of NATO. We exercise and train together more than ever before. Now we want to take the cooperation one step further and integrate the Nordic armed forces even more closely," Sandvik said in a statement.
One particular challenge highlighted by the countries' military leadership was the need to harmonise laws and regulations, for instance when it comes to moving military personnel and equipment across borders.
"We see that there is potential to remove practical obstacles and adapt laws and regulations to make it possible to operate even more smoothly across national borders," said Sandvik.
The move is the latest example of how the Nordic countries are stepping up their defence preparedness, spooked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and uncertainty over the United States as NATO's ultimate security backstop.
All have steeply increased their defence budgets and are now in the top league of defence spenders per capita in NATO.
Norway and Finland both share a land border with Russia.
All of the Nordics are strong backers of Ukraine in its war with Russia. The region has seen a spate of incidents, including drone intrusions, cables and pipelines being sabotaged, that have increased security concerns.
Russia has consistently denied it poses a threat to its Nordic neighbours and regards accusations that it does so as scaremongering. REUTERS

A51.text:
Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
- Published
At least six people have been killed and about 20 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital, the biggest in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.
Eyewitnesses told the BBC that a single missile fired by a warplane hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units overnight.
The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizk Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.
Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".
Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.
Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.
Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.
In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said the missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.
A spokesman for the Civil Defence, which operates under the Hamas-run interior ministry, initially said that five people had been killed and 20 others injured.
Videos shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by the blast.
Local activists have also circulated claims that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.
Speaking to reporters in the aftermath of the strike, the director of Nasser hospital said the building had been hit in a vertical strike, causing extensive damage.
Nasser hospital was hit by a double Israeli strike in August 2025, which killed at least 20 people, including journalists and health workers.
Israeli strikes on Gaza have continued despite a ceasefire agreement in October last year.
More than 1,620 people have been killed since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel and Hamas have accused each other of violating the ceasefire.
The humanitarian crisis in Gaza has recently worsened as a result of heavy rains that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

A52.text:
US envoys arrive in Moscow for Ukraine talks with Vladimir Putin
- Published
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff have arrived in Moscow for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.
Videos shared by Russian media showed Kushner and Witkoff disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.
The American negotiatiors were due to meet Putin at 12:00 local time (09:00 GMT), and will then fly to Dublin to speak to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
On Tuesday, Kushner said the US had seen "some openings and some opportunities" and that they would try to "make some progress" at the meeting with Putin.
The in-person talks with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents were only announced on Wednesday after two days of talks which were framed as centred around the postwar security architecture of Europe.
Nearly five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow shows no sign of backing down from its maximalist demands for sovereign Ukrainian territory and for Western countries to give up any future commitment to protecting Kyiv in case of further attacks.
During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communicatons with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.
However, in recent times many have grown concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin, and have been pushing for a seat at the negotiating table.
The talks in Abu Dhabi were led by the Americans and only included Russia and Ukraine, but Kushner said he and Witkoff would ask Putin to "give his blessing" to invite European representatives in future discussions - particularly with regards to the future configuration of their continent's security architecture.
Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.
But the Russians have been opposed to the idea, citing Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle.
Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, said he thought all parties had "moved closer to achieving peace" but that now "a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the United States, and on whether Europe comes to its senses".
As Witkoff and Kushner were meeting Russian officials in Moscow, Zelensky said Ukraine's military was again facing news of "systematic" restrictions to Starshield satellite internet, Elon Musk's SpaceX service which plays a key role for frontline communications. Connectivity issues in October lasted about a week. Musk denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection.
The restrictions have made it more difficult for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russian jet-powered drones, Zelensky said in a statement.
"This is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," he said.
"We are trying to clear up all circumstances with the American side."

A57.text:
Indonesia's vice-president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
- Published
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka tendered his resignation to parliament on Thursday, triggering the process of finding his replacement amid growing turmoil for the government.
Gibran had been facing impeachment calls after a Supreme Court ruling that a high-school document used during his 2024 election campaign was invalid.
His departure comes amid a faltering political alliance between his father, ex-president Joko Widodo, and the incumbent President Prabowo Subianto.
Standing alongside Gibran, Prabowo told reporters he had accepted his resignation with "a heavy heart". Upper house lawmakers will have 60 days to fill the vacancy from two candidates nominated by the president.
"[Gibran] has demonstrated a chivalrous attitude, a strong sense of responsibility, and the qualities of a statesman," Prabowo said, adding that the resignation was "for the benefit of the nation, the state, and the people of Indonesia".
"He certainly believes that he completed his education through a proper and structured process. However, we must understand that educational systems abroad differ from those in Indonesia," the president said.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
The Supreme Court ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretariat Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
But tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested several senior officials, including presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation to Prabowo - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
[truncated]

A602.text:
Gaming, social media, and e-commerce platforms are facing a fresh wave of sweeping European Union rules that aim to make “your online experience fairer.” The newly proposed Digital Fairness Act (DFA) published by the EU Commission on Wednesday is designed to tackle practices that exploit consumers into spending more of their time and money online, including misleading prices or availability, addictive design features like gaming loot boxes, undisclosed influencer marketing, and more.
Loot boxes, influencers, and addictive features face an EU crackdown
The proposed Digital Fairness Act seeks to bolster consumer protections for online users.
“The Act will protect consumers of all ages shopping and browsing for goods or services online,” the EU Commission said in a news bulletin. “It will also mean fairer competition for businesses, which are expecting to save EU consumers up to €13.7 billion ($15.1 billion) a year.”
Here’s an overview of what the DFA proposal includes:
- A ban on manipulative marketing practices and so-called “dark patterns” that push consumers into making decisions they might not otherwise make, such as fake claims about a product almost being sold out.
- A requirement to give consumers the choice to turn off addictive features, such as persistent prompts, endless scrolling, and autoplay of videos. Restrictions around addictive design also apply to “AI companions and general conversational chatbots.”
- Restrictions on unfair practices that encourage overspending, such as banning gambling-like features (pay-to-win and pay-to-progress, for example) for minors.
- Requiring influencers to clearly disclose advertising content, and restrictions to prevent them from exploiting the trust of children.
- Restrictions on unfair personalised ads and prices that target minors or take advantage of sensitive data.
- Making subscriptions and digital contracts easier to cancel, with prompts to remind customers about upcoming automatic renewals and free trial periods coming to an end.
- Requiring clear and transparent pricing, especially around dynamic pricing and purchases using virtual in-app currency. When consumers wait in virtual queues for cultural and sports event tickets, companies will have to show the current price in real time and at the highest possible price.
- Giving consumers the right to communicate with a human customer service representative, and clear rights using an AI agent to make purchases.
The scope of the restrictions being proposed is broad, and could have a significant impact on major parts of the online digital landscape, from the “rabbit hole” algorithms across YouTube, TikTok, and Meta platforms, to AI chatbots and apps like DuoLingo that relentlessly nudge users to keep interacting with them. Some gaming organizations have already slammed the DFA proposal, describing its restrictions around virtual currencies, loot boxes, and offering micro-transactions to minors as being “unworkable, unjustified and disproportionate.”
Given this is a draft proposal, the DFA will undergo various approvals through the European Parliament and the Council of the European Union before being passed into law, and its current measures could be changed or removed entirely as part of that process. When (or if) it does come into force, the EU Commission says companies who violate the regulations could see fines of up to six percent of their worldwide annual turnover.
“Our consumer protection rules will help ensure that businesses compete on the merits of their products and services - not on their ability to exploit consumers or evade the rules. We are not making it harder to do business. We are making it harder to do business unfairly,” EU Commissioner Michael McGrath said in remarks following the DFA draft publication. “We cannot have 21st-century consumers protected by rules that have not kept pace with the 21st-century economy.”

Finalmente, la junta directiva de Nvidia se prepara para apartar de la empresa a Jensen Huang, su cofundador y director ejecutivo, quien mantuvo una relación extramarital con una presunta espía de China y desató un escándalo que salpicó hasta la Casa Blanca. Según consignó un importante medio financiero, este mismo miércoles los directivos del gigante tecnológico californiano se reúnen para decidir el apartamiento de Huang, mientras las acciones de la empresa sufren caídas de casi 10%.
Huang fundó Nvidia en abril de 1993 y este miércoles, 33 años más tarde, tiene las horas contadas en su junta directiva. Según The Wall Street Journal, la mesa de toma de decisiones del gigante tecnológico con sede en Santa Clara, California, se apresta a apartar a Huang de la empresa. Otro medio, The New York Times, publicó que habría una segunda amante, una directiva de la propia empresa que dependía de él; mientras que Bloomberg sostiene que una consultora extranjera asesora a Nvidia para encontrar un sucesor.
Los coletazos de su affaire sentimental con Alice Huang llegaron muy lejos: grandes desplomes en los valores de las acciones de la empresa y una gran preocupación en el ámbito de la seguridad nacional norteamericana. Este mismo miércoles, mientras se discute desplazarlo de la empresa, las acciones de Nvidia caen alrededor del 8,4 % en el aftermarket.
Según la agencia Bloomberg, la directiva de Nvidia se asesora con una consultora internacional para encontrar al sucesor adecuado para la compañía, así como se estudia la posibilidad de nombrar un director interino mientras busca uno permanente.
El domingo, Huang reconoció en una carta a sus empleados que le había sido infiel a su esposa y se disculpó por haber traicionado la confianza de los integrantes de la compañía. La relación extramarital involucraba a Alice Huang, ejecutiva de Megaspeed, una empresa de gestión de datos con sede en Singapur y que fue en el pasado un importante cliente de Nvidia. Según funcionarios de inteligencia estadounidenses, trabaja para los servicios de inteligencia chinos.
Durante la semana se dieron a conocer más datos sobre el affaire, así como también el detalle importante de que se desconoce el paradero de Alice Huang. Más aún, el propio Donald Trump aseguró a inicios de esta semana que habló con Jensen Huang para conocer su estado de ánimo y señaló que el todavía CEO de Nvidia le juró que no estaba al tanto de que su amante habría estado colaborando con Beijing, así como también que él le cree.
Pero el affaire con Alice Huang no habría sido el único que se consigna en versiones que comienzan a salir a la luz desde el propio interior de Nvidia. Es que el medio The New York Times publicó este mismo miércoles que, según cinco trabajadores de la empresa, Jensen Huang también mantuvo una relación extramatrimonial con una ejecutiva que dependía directamente de él.
"La relación, que no se había dado a conocer anteriormente, era con Kimberly Powell, vicepresidenta de salud de Nvidia, según informaron fuentes que hablaron bajo condición de anonimato para describir información sensible", consignó el medio neoyorquino.

El contexto de una eventual salida de Huang

A92.text:
El embajador ruso en Washington, Alexandr Dárichev, murió este miércoles de forma repentina a los 66 años de edad, informó la Cancillería rusa en un comunicado.
"La dirección y el personal del Ministerio de Exteriores de Rusia anuncian con profundo pesar el repentino fallecimiento de Alexandr Dárichev, embajador extraordinario y plenipotenciario de la Federación Rusa ante Estados Unidos, ocurrido el 11 de noviembre a la edad de 66 años", señala la nota oficial.
El comunicado destaca que Dárichev era "un diplomático excepcional, un líder experimentado, un buen amigo y un mentor".
"Profesional de primer nivel y brillante experto en asuntos estadounidenses, Alexandr Dárichev desempeñó un papel fundamental en una de las áreas más importantes de la política exterior rusa", concluye la nota.
Dárichev era hijo del que fue consejero de la embajada rusa en Hungría, Nikita Dárichev, y comenzó su propia carrera diplomática en la década de los 1990.
Trabajó durante largos períodos en la embajada rusa en Estados Unidos y también encabezó la misión diplomática de su país en Canadá.
Dárichev fue además subdirector del Departamento de América del Norte en el Ministerio de Exteriores ruso.
En marzo de 2025, en el marco de un acercamiento entre Rusia y Estados Unidos tras la vuelta de Donald Trump a la Casa Blanca, fue nombrado jefe de la misión diplomática rusa en Washington, ocupando un cargo que se mantenía vacante desde octubre de 2024.
Dárichiev nació el 14 de mayo de 1960 en el seno de una familia de diplomáticos en Hungría. Estudió historia en la Facultad de Historia de la Universidad Estatal de Moscú, donde se graduó en 1983, y aprendió a hablar inglés y francés con fluidez.
Fue becario del Instituto de Estudios Estadounidenses y Canadienses de la Academia de Ciencias Soviética durante la década de 1980, antes de incorporarse al Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores ruso en 1992, justo después de la disolución de la Unión Soviética. Trabajó en su Departamento de América del Norte durante toda su carrera.

A98.text:
China views democratically-governed Taiwan as its own territory, despite Taipei's strong rejection of that claim, and has repeatedly offered a "one country, two systems" model of autonomy not supported by any major Taiwanese political party.
Resolving the Taiwan question is an "unwavering historical mission" of China's Communist Party, Xi said in a speech in Beijing's Great Hall of the People.
"The tide of history cannot be stopped," Xi added. "The complete reunification of the motherland must be realised, and it will certainly be realised."
Taiwan's government dismissed the remarks.
Its Mainland Affairs Council said neither the government nor Taiwan's people could accept "one country, two systems," which would ultimately mean submitting to the Communist Party's authoritarian rule.
"As for the wording on Taiwan unification, it isn't much different from the past," council spokesperson Liang Wen-chieh told reporters.
Xi's comments came in a speech on the 160th birthday of revolutionary hero Sun Yat-sen who helped lead a 1911 revolt that ended centuries of rule by emperors and empresses and ushered in the Republic of China.
Xi said China adheres to "peaceful reunification and the policy of 'one country, two systems'" and is willing to talk to Taiwan while upholding the "one-China principle", or Beijing's position that both sides of the Taiwan Strait are one country.
All Chinese, including those in Taiwan, should join hands to jointly oppose Taiwan independence "separatist" forces and strive for peaceful development of cross-Strait ties, Xi added.
Despite Xi not mentioning the use of force, which China has never renounced for Taiwan, its military operates around the island on a daily basis, and is extending its reach further into the Pacific.
Taiwan's defence ministry said it had detected 29 Chinese military aircraft, including J-16 fighter jets and drones, carrying out a "joint combat readiness patrol" around Taiwan in conjunction with Chinese warships, starting on Thursday.
TAIWAN TELLS PEOPLE TO STAY AWAY
Xi's speech comes a week ahead of the APEC summit in China's southern tech hub of Shenzhen, where he is due to again meet US President Donald Trump, and also a little more than two weeks before important local elections in Taiwan.
Last month, Taiwan called on its people to steer clear of any of China's events to mark the Sun anniversary, saying China had a distorted view of him and his legacy.
Beijing calls Sun a great national hero and patriot, as well as the forerunner of the 1949 communist revolution that forced the defeated Republic of China government to flee to Taiwan, where it remains to this day.
Xi said Sun was a great national hero, a great patriot and a "great pioneer of China's democratic revolution".
"Mr. Sun Yat-sen consistently upheld the unity of the country and the solidarity of the nation, and he firmly opposed all words and actions that split the country or the nation," he added.
'FATHER OF THE NATION'
In Taiwan, Sun is officially considered the "father of the nation" and his portrait hangs in the presidential office, though his political philosophy, "Three Principles of the People", is no longer a required text for schoolchildren.
While Taiwan President Lai Ching-te and his ruling Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan's separate identity from China, they have been striking a tougher tone with Beijing on the role of the Republic of China.
Taiwan has been particularly upset by Beijing's effort to claim credit for the victory in World War Two, saying it was the Republic of China government that fought alongside the allies, as the People's Republic of China did not exist at the time.
China says Lai is a "separatist" and has refused to speak with him. Lai says only Taiwan's people can decide their future.
(Reporting by Beijing newsroom; Additional reporting by Ben Blanchard and Yimou Lee in Taipei; Editing by Christian Schmollinger, Clarence Fernandez and Thomas Derpinghaus)

A101.text:
The expression of support after the departure of Gibran Rakabuming Raka, Indonesia's highest profile resignation since that of President Suharto in 1998, could soothe signs of strain in the political alliance of Prabowo and predecessor Widodo.
"We will continue to support President Prabowo's administration, especially programmes that serve the interests of the broader public," the highly popular Widodo, known as Jokowi, told reporters outside his home in Solo in central Java.
The rift between Prabowo and Jokowi, who twice defeated the powerful former general for the presidency before throwing him support in the face of term limits, had looked set to further destabilise the government, analysts said.
Prabowo's government is battling scandals over signature political programmes and doubts about its prowess to manage Southeast Asia's biggest economy, where the political turmoil has sapped investor sentiment.
Scrutiny is growing over the government's fiscal plans and broader policy direction, while downgrade risks still linger for the stock market, with the rupiah IDR= weakening about 0.6% to plumb a fresh record low of 18,255 against the dollar.
Minutes before Jokowi's remarks, Gibran arrived at parliament in Jakarta, the capital, where he met leaders for 20 minutes, handing in his resignation and asking parliament to process it, said Ahmad Muzani, the speaker of the upper house.
Gibran made his decision "through my own volition ... for the interests of the government and nation," Muzani told reporters while reading out the resignation letter.
Senior law minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra said Gibran quit for personal reasons and cited "growing public sentiment", in the letter of just five paragraphs.
CALLS FOR IMPEACHMENT BEFORE RESIGNATION
Gibran had also submitted a resignation letter to Prabowo, said Muzani, adding that he did not explain why he resigned.
The 39-year-old was elected alongside Prabowo in a 2024 election, during which Jokowi was accused of meddling in the process by influencing a court decision that changed the election rules, enabling Gibran to stand.
His resignation followed a push by lawmakers for Gibran's impeachment on grounds of inadequate educational credentials.
It also followed rulings by the Constitutional Court and the Supreme Court that his overseas high school qualifications fell short of legal requirements for vice presidential candidates, and had been wrongly accepted by election authorities.
PRESIDENT EXPECTED TO SUBMIT TWO REPLACEMENT CANDIDATES
Parliamentary leaders will now gather to discuss the next steps, Muzani said.
The upper house will have to hold a session to declare a vacancy after Gibran's resignation, while sending the president a letter seeking the names of two replacement candidates, senior law minister Yusril Ihza Mahendra said on Wednesday.
An upper house election will follow within 60 days.
Analysts said another sign of the gulf between Prabowo and Jokowi was last week's revelation of an inquiry into illegal wiretapping by senior police officials, including former police chief Listyo Sigit Prabowo, widely seen as a Jokowi loyalist.
On Thursday, police said they had enough initial evidence to pursue treason charges against four suspects for wiretapping Prabowo, other politicians, activists and journalists.
At a hearing, lawmakers urged police chief Suyudi Ario Seto to uncover who ultimately ordered Listyo to conduct the alleged wiretapping, and the political interests that could be behind it.
(Reporting by Ananda Teresia; Writing by Gayatri Suroyo; Editing by David Stanway and Clarence Fernandez)

A129.text:
Nach Trump-Aussagen Iran droht mit Angriffen auf US-Stützpunkte auch in Europa
Die Führung von Iran warnt die USA vor neuen Angriffen auf die Islamische Republik. »Wenn die USA einen weiteren Krieg gegen Iran beginnen, wird jeder Militärstützpunkt, der an der Aggression beteiligt ist – von Westasien bis Europa – ein legitimes Ziel für die tödlichen Angriffe Irans sein«, schrieb der Generalsekretär des iranischen Sicherheitsrats, Mohsen Rezaee, auf der Plattform X. Es werde dann keine sichere Entfernung, keinen sicheren Zufluchtsort, keine Immunität geben, drohte er.
Vor wenigen Tagen hatte US-Präsident Donald Trump die militärische Auseinandersetzung mit Iran für »effektiv vorüber« erklärt und gesagt: »Wir halten den Status quo aufrecht, und das tun wir auf Drängen der Nachbarländer.«
»Weder Krieg noch Frieden«
Dagegen sagte der iranische Parlamentspräsident Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf dem Sender Al Jazeera, sein Land sei entschlossen, den als »weder Krieg noch Frieden« beschriebenen Zustand zu überwinden – nicht unbedingt durch Verhandlungen, sondern durch nachhaltige Abschreckung. Eine Einigung mit Washington sei möglich, der Ball liege bei den USA. Bislang habe Trumps Regierung auf die iranische Botschaft aber nicht konkret geantwortet. Ghalibaf wies erneut auf sieben Bedingungen hin, die die USA erfüllen müssten, damit Iran die Straße von Hormus öffnen und Verhandlungen aufnehmen werde.
Berichten zufolge sollen die USA nach Vorstellung Teherans unter anderem alle Kampfhandlungen gegen Iran und dessen Verbündete in der Region, wie die Hisbollah im Libanon, einstellen. Außerdem sollen die Seeblockade gegen iranische Häfen und Schiffe beendet, Sanktionen sowie das Verbot von Ölexporten aufgehoben und eingefrorene iranische Vermögenswerte freigegeben werden. Iran verlangt demnach auch Reparationen für Kriegsschäden. Es gilt als unwahrscheinlich, dass die US-Regierung diese Forderungen vorab erfüllen wird.
Derweil teilte das zuständige Regionalkommando des US-Militärs mit, die amerikanischen Streitkräfte arbeiteten weiter daran, die Straße von Hormus für den Handelsschiffverkehr offenzuhalten und die »eiserne Seeblockade« gegen Iran strikt durchzusetzen.
Ende Februar hatten Israel und die USA ihren Krieg gegen Iran begonnen. Als Reaktion blockierten Irans Streitkräfte mit Drohungen und Angriffen über lange Zeit faktisch den Schiffsverkehr in der Straße von Hormus. Seit mehreren Monaten versucht die US-Marine, mit Geleitschutz für zivile Schiffe den Handel mit Öl und Flüssiggas über die Meerenge wieder zu ermöglichen.

Kyiv and Moscow on Wednesday agreed to a large-scale prisoner exchange as the final day of peace talks in Abu Dhabi came to an end, though neither side gave a concrete figure. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will meet separately with Russian President Vladimir Putin and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday.
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner will separately meet Russia's Vladimir Putin and Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday as they seek to seize "openings" from two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on ending the Ukraine war.
The two men will travel first to Moscow to meet the Russian president, before flying to Dublin – where Zelensky will attend European meetings – to debrief the Ukrainian leader.
Arriving in Ireland, Zelensky said there could be a "window of opportunity" to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II before 2027.
"What's important is that the Americans flew to Putin with specifics. I would very much like them to return to Dublin with specifics," he said, adding that, while he was still sceptical, "there is hope".
He also welcomed what he called "change in tone" from the US on the prospect of Europe's inclusion in the Washington-mediated talks, saying the "American side is treating it more positively, more warmly."

European countries have been rattled by Russia pushing a review of the entire continent's security architecture, with the US also floating a new framework.
Moscow's chief negotiator said Wednesday the Kremlin aimed for a "new, modern Yalta" – referring to the 1945 conference in which Western leaders carved up Europe with the Soviet Union.
Some 50 European leaders are due to gather in the Irish capital Thursday, with the Abu Dhabi talks set to dominate the summit.
EU officials say there appears to have been little genuine progress towards peace and are adamant that Europe sees no need to discuss its broader security arrangement with Moscow before fighting stops.
NATO chief Mark Rutte however said Wednesday that the Abu Dhabi talks showed the US, Ukraine and Europe were "aligned and united".
'Biggest' prisoner exchange
Zelensky and the US have called on Europe to choose who will represent it at the talks – but European officials said they did not expect the leaders to take any decisions on naming a single envoy for any potential talks with the Kremlin.

Zelensky said Kyiv was waiting for a response from Moscow on a possible POW exchange that could be "1,000 for 1,000, maybe it will even come to 1,200".
