A198.text:
Nvidia Corp. was under growing pressure late Wednesday to remove chief executive Jensen Huang after reports that he had two affairs, one with an executive reporting to him and another with an alleged Chinese spy.
The semiconductor giant is now confronting nervous markets, geopolitical intrigue and concerns about the fallout for the entire artificial intelligence industry.
On Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia’s board was meeting and preparing to oust the company’s founder and public face.
The company supplies most of the chips and hundreds of billions of dollars driving the current AI boom. Mr. Huang, 63, is one of the technology industry’s most recognizable and powerful figures, and a leader who has helped define today’s AI sector. His exit would leave a vacuum at the top of the industry.
China says it doesn’t use ‘honeytraps’ – but warns citizens against seductive foreign spies
Nvidia’s directors had launched an independent investigation into Mr. Huang on Sunday, after claims that he had been the subject of a foreign intelligence effort. The same day, the chief executive acknowledged he had been unfaithful in his marriage. The other person involved in the extramarital affair has been identified as Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International, a provider of AI infrastructure.
The U.S. Commerce Department had been investigating whether Megaspeed helped circumvent export controls by moving Nvidia’s specialized AI chips to China. Megaspeed has said it follows the law and denied any illicit hardware transfers. A Trump administration memo had also identified Ms. Huang as an asset of Beijing’s security ministry, The New York Times reported. China has denied any such spying.
On Wednesday, The Times also reported that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of health care.
The Globe and Mail has not independently verified the reports. Nvidia did not immediately respond to The Globe’s request for comment.
Nvidia’s shares have whipsawed this week after Mr. Huang’s first affair admission. On Wednesday evening, its stock price fell sharply in after-hours trading following reports that Mr. Huang could exit and leave behind a leadership vacuum.
Nvidia, and Mr. Huang, have been integral to the development and success of the AI sector.
The Taiwan-born electrical engineer co-founded the company in 1993, and it became a leading maker of graphics hardware used in gaming computers. But in the late 2000s, computer science researchers began using Nvidia graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models, then an out-of-favour form of AI.
In 2012, University of Toronto professor Geoffrey Hinton and his students Ilya Sutskever and Alex Krizhevsky proved the power of that approach with a major breakthrough in image recognition; their model was trained on Nvidia GPUs. Mr. Hinton went on to co-win the Nobel Prize for his work on AI, while Mr. Sutskever co-founded OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT. He has since departed to launch the startup Safe Superintelligence Inc., which aims to develop systems that exceed human smarts.
Today, Nvidia is by far the market leader in the computing hardware that’s used to train and run the most advanced AI models. The firm reported a US$118-billion net profit on just under US$178-billion in revenue across the two fiscal quarters ending July 26. That was up from US$45-billion and almost US$91-billion, respectively, over the same period last year. Nvidia’s hardware is a hot commodity for cloud providers, and it typically makes up the largest single cost for all the new AI data centres being built around the world.
In addition to selling the GPUs that fuel the AI boom, Nvidia is helping to fund many of the developers driving it. The California-based company has committed tens of billions of dollars each to OpenAI and chief rival Anthropic.

Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S.-mediated talks concluded with no major breakthrough on ending Moscow’s nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion.
Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.
U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington’s peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.
Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement.
U.S. envoys to meet with Putin and Zelensky
The sides last met in February on Russia’s invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.
The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day.
“One of the positives is we agreed that we’re going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we’re going to finalize the numbers tomorrow,” said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended.
Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv’s contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted the agreement was “in principle.”
Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff’s information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps since 1,000 soldiers from each side returned home last year.
The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said.
Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The Ukrainian leader gave a muted welcome to the outcome of the talks, saying a proposed prisoner exchange was a positive step. But he said Ukraine will not give in to demands that it cede its territory that has been occupied by Russia in exchange for peace.
Medinsky said he felt the talks helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described them as “substantive and quite useful.”

Umerov said Kyiv’s delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks.
Moscow doesn’t want European countries, which are concerned about Russia’s conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks.
Despite that. he said there had been a “change in temperature,” with Washington warming to the idea of a European role.
“Ending this war without Europe’s participation would be unjust, and it would be impossible,” Zelensky said through an interpreter.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements “don’t indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace.” Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine.
Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps.
[truncated]

A21.text:
Iran warns of expanded retaliation as Israel reportedly readies to attack
Israeli security cabinet orders military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran, Israeli media reports.
Israel has reportedly ordered its military to step up readiness for possible strikes on Iran as Tehran warned it would expand the war beyond the region if attacked.
Israel’s security cabinet, chaired by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, has ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran, Israeli media reported on Wednesday evening.
“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.
KAN said the directives were made public after Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot issued a statement telling Netanyahu – who is serving as prime minister in a caretaker capacity – not to deploy the military “without a direct and immediate threat” until the next government is formed.
Eisenkot was offered the chance to form a new government by Israeli President Isaac Herzog over the weekend after Netanyahu’s ruling coalition lost its parliamentary majority in the October elections.
Netanyahu, who is on the cusp of losing power if the opposition succeeds in forming a government, has been adamant that the war on Iran will continue until the collapse of the government in Tehran.
‘From West Asia to Europe’
Reports of Israeli preparations to attack Iran come at a time of intense diplomatic efforts to avert further conflict and reach a diplomatic solution.
US President Donald Trump has said that he is prepared to return to waging war if a diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to facilitate a deal between Washington and Tehran.
Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei said in a social media post, “If the US launches another war against Iran, every military base involved in the aggression, from West Asia to Europe, will be a legitimate target for Iran’s lethal strikes.”
“No safe distance. No safe haven. No immunity,” he added.
Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar Atas, reporting from Tehran, said the Iranian leadership has been discussing whether or not to appoint the hawkish Rezaei as Iran’s new chief negotiator.
“In Tehran, there have been voices saying that if this status quo goes on for quite a long period of time, Iran will not wait and might take pre-emptive action,” Atas said, adding that the current lead negotiator, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, has commented on Iran’s determination to move beyond this state of “no war, no peace” through “sustainable deterrence” if negotiations fail.
Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview published on Wednesday that the Strait of Hormuz will “never return” to its status prior to the US-Israel war on Iran and that “the ball is now in the American court”.
“What stands in the way of an agreement is our lack of trust in the United States,” he said.
‘Position to declare victory’
In Washington, DC, Al Jazeera’s Alan Fisher said Trump is still justifying why he went to war with Iran and saying that it would end soon.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also said the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign against Iran is proving so effective that a resumption of large-scale military operations is unnecessary.
“Over the last few days, both the president and Marco Rubio have said, effectively, that large-scale military engagement is over. They do not see the need to restart it unless Iran crosses red lines,” Fisher said, adding that the “key issue for this White House is always to be in a position where Trump can declare victory”.
“But it is clear there is some movement behind the scenes as far as negotiating a settlement,” he said.
Despite the push for peace, US forces “continue to work around the clock” in keeping the Strait of Hormuz open for commercial shipping, strictly enforcing the “ironclad” naval blockade against Iran, according to the US Central Command.
[truncated]

A284.text:
Israeli strike on a Gaza hospital kills 6 people, health authorities say
KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip — An Israeli airstrike targeting the Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a general surgeon, and wounded at least a dozen more, Gaza's Health Ministry said.
The strike was carried out early Thursday, according to the Israeli military, which said it struck a Hamas commander and other militants, without providing evidence.
The Gaza Health Ministry said the strike hit the hospital's surgical wing and that a doctor, Rizk Abu Shaira, was among the dead. Inside the building, parts of several floors were either severely damaged or destroyed. Debris was scattered across hospital beds and equipment, and rebar dangled from the ceiling where the munition penetrated.
Nasser Hospital in the city of Khan Younis is one of the few functioning medical facilities left in Gaza, whose healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war.
The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across Gaza, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. It has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.
In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it used for military purposes.
In a statement on Thursday, the military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."
Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed five journalists — including AP contributor Mariam Dagga — when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex.
The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, which is part of the Hamas-run government but whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.
Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

A286.text:
Russia and Ukraine agree to a prisoner exchange as talks end with no big breakthrough
ABU DHABI, United Arab Emirates — Russia and Ukraine agreed to a large exchange of prisoners of war, both sides said Wednesday as two days of U.S. mediated talks concluded with no major breakthrough on ending Moscow's nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion.
Hopes had been low for any significant development in the first meeting in nine months between the delegations. Russia and Ukraine have from time to time swapped POWs but have remained far apart in their demands for accepting a peace settlement.
U.S. officials say they are determined to revive Washington's peace efforts that so far have failed to deliver significant results.
Along with postwar security guarantees for both countries, other key hurdles are the fate of Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory and what role European countries will play in an eventual settlement.
U.S. envoys to meet with Putin and Zelenskyy
The session was the first such meeting since February on Russia's invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.
The talks lasted just under two hours Wednesday, after a four-hour session the previous day.
"One of the positives is we agreed that we're going to have the biggest humanitarian release of prisoners, which we're going to finalize the numbers tomorrow," said Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump's son-in-law, after the Abu Dhabi talks ended.
Vladimir Medinsky, head of the Russian delegation, and Rustem Umerov, who led Kyiv's contingent, confirmed the planned POW exchange, although Medinsky noted the agreement was "in principle."
Alexander Zorin, a deputy chief of the General Staff's information department who attended the talks, told Russian state TV it would be one of the biggest such swaps after the 1,000 soldiers returned home last year.
The latest exchange could take place in the next two or three weeks, he said.
Kushner said he and U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will travel to Moscow on Thursday to meet with President Vladimir Putin, then fly to Dublin, Ireland, to meet Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Medinsky said he felt the meeting helped Moscow and Kyiv edge closer to peace, while Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "substantive and quite useful."
European officials were excluded by Moscow from the talks
Umerov said Kyiv's delegation was expected to meet later Wednesday with representatives of European governments, the European Union and NATO who were in the capital of the United Arab Emirates but did not attend the three-way talks.
Moscow doesn't want European countries, which are concerned about Russia's conduct and broader intentions on the continent, involved in the direct negotiations. Kushner said one of the goals of the Moscow meeting is to try to get Europeans added to the talks.
"Ukraine's priority is to end the war as soon as possible with a dignified peace," Zelenskyy said on X. "We believe that Europe must be represented at every stage of real diplomacy. It is essential that the United States have a strong position and exert influence on the source of this war — that is Russia."
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said European representatives could eventually join peace talks but added their current statements "don't indicate any desire on their part to contribute to movement along the path toward peace." Moscow complains that Europe is financing and supplying weaponry to Ukraine.
Kushner said both Ukraine and Russia needed clarity on postwar security arrangements. He said European countries, the EU and NATO have to be involved in those discussions to build consensus on next steps.
Ukraine wants to ensure that Moscow doesn't invade again, and EU officials say any discussions on Europe's security arrangements could only start after a ceasefire.
[truncated]

A476.text:
US envoys arrive in Moscow for latest round of Ukrainian peace talks with Putin
MOSCOW, Nov 12 - US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday for talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, part of their latest push for a peace deal in Ukraine.
The Kremlin talks - expected to take place in the first half of the day - will be the 10th time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, and follow two days of trilateral peace talks in Abu Dhabi which finished on Wednesday with news of another planned major prisoner exchange but no public breakthrough in wider negotiations.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special envoy, met Kushner and Witkoff off their plane amid wet snow and accompanied them to central Moscow ahead of their talks with Putin.
This week's Abu Dhabi talks were the first direct negotiations between Russia and Ukraine mediated by the US to try to end the 4-1/2-year-old war in nine months and, although Russian and Ukrainian negotiators reported some progress, the US side said differences remained on major issues, including territory.
Despite public optimism from US President Trump, there has been no sign of major compromises.
Kyiv has strongly rejected Putin's demands to surrender the whole of the eastern region of Donbas in return for peace, and with talks deadlocked on land, US mediators have tried to steer discussions towards postwar security guarantees and reconstruction.
A senior Russian diplomat said on Wednesday that Moscow could conclude non-aggression pacts with NATO member states as part of a new security architecture for Europe, though many European politicians say they oppose any discussion of Europe's overall security before real progress on Ukraine - including a ceasefire - is made. REUTERS

A484.text:
This trader raised alarm about Nvidia’s China entanglements months ago
Rob Copeland and Maureen Farrell
- Christian Lamarco, a short seller at Culper Research, warned months ago about Nvidia’s China business and Jensen Huang’s link to Megaspeed worker Alice Huang.

A486.text:
Russia, Ukraine exchange attacks on capitals as US envoys land in Moscow
- Russia and Ukraine traded attacks on Kyiv and Moscow on 12 November, just after peace talks ended and as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow.
- Russia said it hit military and energy sites in Ukraine, while Kyiv reported explosions, damaged power and civilian infrastructure, and a drone strike threat near Moscow.
- Talks in Abu Dhabi led to a prisoner exchange, but major gaps remain on territory. The US envoys will next meet President Volodymyr Zelensky in Ireland.

Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on each other’s capitals early on Nov 12, a day after peace talks ended and shortly before US envoys arrived in Moscow to meet President Vladimir Putin.
Kirill Dmitriev, Putin’s envoy, greeted US negotiators Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff at a Moscow airport, ahead of their meeting with the Kremlin chief later in the day.
“Welcoming Steve and Jared to Moscow,” Dmitriev said on X, posting a picture of himself shaking hands with Witkoff near a plane on a grey wintery morning, Kushner standing alongside.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators agreed to a prisoner exchange during two days of peace talks in Abu Dhabi that ended on Nov 11, but US mediators said differences remained on major issues, including territorial questions.
Kushner has said European partners must be at the Russia-Ukraine negotiating table.
The Russian Defence Ministry said on Telegram it had hit military and energy facilities in Ukraine as well as a munitions warehouse in the capital Kyiv.
Explosions were heard in Kyiv in the early hours of Nov 12, a Reuters witness said. The attacks damaged energy and civilian infrastructure in the Rivne region, a local official said on Telegram.
Russia downed five drones that were heading for Moscow, Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Telegram on Nov 12. Other drones were downed in a number of Russian regions, including Rostov and Tula, local officials said.
When they leave Moscow, the US negotiators plan to fly to Ireland to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who is due to attend a meeting of European leaders there. REUTERS

A487.text:
Nvidia working with outside firm to identify CEO candidates
- Nvidia’s board is using an outside firm to find possible replacements for CEO Jensen Huang after reports of multiple affairs and a possible spying link.
- Directors are considering a temporary chief, while the company faces pressure from investors, staff and lawmakers over trade secrets and succession planning.
- The crisis hit Nvidia’s share price, which fell 8% after reports, and raised wider concerns because Huang has led the firm through its huge rise in value.
AI generated
Nvidia’s board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for chief executive Jensen Huang following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman who is reportedly suspected of spying for China, a person familiar with the situation said.
The board is weighing the idea of naming a temporary chief while searching for a permanent one, the person said, asking not to be identified because the information is not public.
Directors were meeting on Nov 11 to discuss Huang’s fate, according to people familiar with the situation.
The Wall Street Journal said earlier that the board was preparing to oust Huang, citing unidentified people familiar with the matter.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia’s board has been facing a succession crisis since Nov 8 when Huang admitted that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a data centre executive at a company that is one of Nvidia’s largest South-east Asian customers.
The New York Times has reported that Alice Huang was suspected of operating as an agent on behalf of the Chinese government.
The crisis escalated late on Nov 11, when the Times reported that Jensen Huang also had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, citing unidentified people who worked at the company.
Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The disclosure and subsequent reports have left the board with a difficult option: ousting the founder and only person to have run Nvidia, firing an executive who – at least until recently – had commanded widespread respect of shareholders and customers alike, and who had overseen a surge of more than 700,000% in the company’s share price.
But keeping Jensen Huang in the role would likely subject Nvidia to a barrage of scrutiny from lawmakers, investors, customers and staff concerned over his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it put Nvidia’s trade secrets at risk – as well as his extramarital relationship with a person who directly reported to him at the company.
The developments have also shined a light on Nvidia’s lack of a succession plan for Huang, and reinforced how inseparable the 63-year-old CEO is from the company and its success.
His potential exit would reverberate far beyond the company’s operations, and not just because Nvidia is the dominant maker of chips at the heart of the AI boom.
Huang is a consummate dealmaker and has used the company’s vast resources to invest in the AI supply chain and a variety of start-ups.
He is also a top evangelist for the AI revolution itself, downplaying fears about the risks to humanity and talking up the benefits.
The company’s stock dropped 8% in extended trading following the reports on Nov 11.
Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm that was spun out of a Chinese gaming enterprise.
That company has been under US investigation for months related to potential chip smuggling, Bloomberg has reported.
Megaspeed and Nvidia have denied wrongdoing, and Beijing has dismissed allegations that it spied on Jensen Huang. BLOOMBERG

A488.text:
Saudi Arabia says debris from intercepted missiles falls in Mecca region
- Saudi Arabia said debris from two intercepted ballistic missiles fell in the Mecca region on Nov 11, near the Grand Mosque, after air defence destroyed them.
- Saudi civil defence called it a “hostile targeting of civilian objects” and a “flagrant violation of international humanitarian law”; the Houthis denied targeting Mecca and Medina.
- The attack adds to the Yemen war’s escalation, which resumed in 2026 and now threatens the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route.
AI generated
DUBAI – Saudi Arabia said debris from two ballistic missiles intercepted by its air defences fell in the Mecca region on Nov 11, as the kingdom and Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued to trade attacks in an escalating conflict.
Saudi state television identified the locations as Sabuhah village, about 35km north-east of the Grand Mosque in Mecca, and Wadi al-Maghmas, about 21km east of the mosque.
The missiles were launched towards the region and intercepted and destroyed, Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said in a statement.
The Houthis have repeatedly denied Saudi accusations that they target Mecca and Medina, Islam’s two holiest cities, saying their military operations are directed at military and strategic targets elsewhere in Saudi Arabia.
Mecca, home to sites sacred to Muslims worldwide, is the focal point of the annual hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims undertake each year.
“This hostile targeting of civilian objects constitutes a flagrant violation of international humanitarian law and reflects the dangerous hostile approach pursued by the Houthi militia,” Saudi Arabia’s civil defence said early on Nov 12.
The Houthis seized Yemen’s capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting Saudi Arabia to intervene militarily the following year in support of the internationally recognised government.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely froze the conflict, but hostilities resumed earlier in 2026, with the Houthis launching missile and drone attacks on Saudi territory and Riyadh carrying out air strikes in Yemen.
The latest escalation has threatened the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. REUTERS

A490.text:
Why Nvidia matters and what’s now at stake
- Nvidia’s value fell after reports linked CEO Jensen Huang to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. Huang admitted an extramarital affair, and China called the spy claim “unsubstantiated”.
- Nvidia became a market giant after ChatGPT boosted demand for its AI chips. Its shares rose fourteen-fold, and it passed US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market value in 2025.
- The scandal raises “key-man” risk because Huang drives major decisions and has no named successor. Nvidia also faces tougher chip competition, especially in China, and its huge S&P 500 weight affects many investors.
AI generated
NEW YORK – It is not often that a revelation about a relationship erases a trillion dollars of value from the stock market. But that is what has happened in the wake of media reports that a woman suspected of being an asset for Chinese intelligence had grown close to Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, who acknowledged having an extramarital affair.
The wipeout speaks both to the chipmaker’s sheer size – at around US$4 trillion (S$5.1 trillion), Nvidia’s market capitalisation is comparable to the national economic output of Japan, the UK or India – and to the pivotal role of its leather-jacketed, celebrity CEO.
It was Huang’s decision to pivot Nvidia’s focus from graphics chips for gaming to the artificial intelligence “accelerators” that have made it one the world’s biggest companies by market value, and his globe-trotting lobbying has helped to maintain its dominant position.
Hence the sharp sell-off of Nvidia’s shares when the espionage scandal raised questions about his future at the company. A spokesman for China’s government called the “so-called Chinese spy allegation” unsubstantiated.
Here is why the stakes are so high.
Market titan
On Nov 30, 2022, a then-little-known company called OpenAI released a chatbot called ChatGPT, triggering an explosion in demand for a type of computing chip that Nvidia was uniquely well-placed to provide. After that, Nvidia’s share price rose fourteen-fold to a peak on Oct 6.
The company witnessed soaring demand from data-centre customers, including Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft. In mid-2024, it overtook all three by market capitalisation for the first time. In 2025, Nvidia became the first company to surpass both US$4 trillion and US$5 trillion in market value.
By early October, it was closing in on the US$6 trillion mark. Since then, it has fallen behind Apple as the world’s biggest company. Investors have become increasingly skittish over frothy AI stock valuations and an industry borrowing spree. And the Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections has cast doubt over the sustainability of an AI data centre construction boom. By Nov 10, the revelations about Huang’s affair had pushed Nvidia’s valuation to a level almost on a par with the No. 3 company, Microsoft.
Chip supremacy
Nvidia today accounts for an overwhelming share of sales of the advanced chips that process AI tasks. Its dominance partly reflects a substantial head start: Years before AI really took off, the company was investing in ways to use its graphics processing units for uses beyond gaming. It has maintained that lead by rolling out new designs every year. Its size and purchasing power have kept it ahead of the game, making it harder for smaller rivals to keep up.
Now is a particularly bad time for the company to be risking a leadership crisis. Nvidia’s rivals, and even some of its customers, are working hard to develop competitive AI chips. A raft of start-ups are raising billions of dollars from investors keen to back the next breakthrough. Competition is also intensifying in China, where the company is prevented by US export controls from selling its most advanced products. Companies such as Huawei Technologies – blacklisted in the US – are making rapid strides in developing homegrown AI chips, Nvidia has said.
[truncated]

A495.text:
Tech allies rally behind Jensen Huang, calling him vital in AI race
Emmy Martin
- Silicon Valley investors backed Jensen Huang after his admission of infidelity and links to an accused Chinese spy, saying he is vital to America’s AI leadership.
- Supporters, including Elon Musk and Bill Ackman, called Huang “irreplaceable” and warned that losing Nvidia’s chief would help China in the AI race.
- Nvidia’s board has opened an investigation, Congress wants a closed-door briefing, and Trump said, “I really believe him,” while Beijing denied the spying claims.
AI generated
SAN FRANCISCO – Within hours of Jensen Huang’s admission on Nov 8 that he had been unfaithful to his wife, some of Silicon Valley’s most influential investors closed ranks around him.
Their messages, delivered mostly on social media, were consistent. Huang’s relationship with a woman identified by US officials as a Chinese spy was a personal failing. Losing the Nvidia chief executive, they argued, would be a far bigger blow to the country, and America could not win the artificial intelligence race without him.
“Jensen is one of the greatest entrepreneurs of this generation,” Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, wrote in a post on the afternoon of Nov 8. He said that Huang “did something incredibly dumb” and that it was bad for America, “but my guess is there was no bad intention”.
He concluded that Huang is “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership”.
About an hour later, Elon Musk quoted the post and added: “I agree.”
The show of loyalty reflects Huang’s rarefied standing in Silicon Valley. In the three decades since he co-founded Nvidia, he has gone from running a maker of video game graphics cards to presiding over the company at the centre of the AI boom, now one of the world’s most valuable companies.
Nvidia’s chips are the scarce resource every AI company needs, a position that makes Huang something of a kingmaker. Decisions about who gets his products, and how many, can shape which start-ups and tech giants pull ahead. Nvidia’s finances are also deeply intertwined with other leading AI companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic.
(China has rejected the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.)
Bill Ackman, a billionaire hedge fund manager, called Jensen Huang “an incredible human” who took “full responsibility as he should” and urged people to “support him and his family”. Later on Nov 8, Ackman added that he was “not suggesting he gets a free pass”.
On Nov 9, investor Gavin Baker argued that many venture capitalists were “patriotic Americans” who believed Huang’s policy views served the country against China. He wrote that it would be “a disaster for America – and a gift to China – if Jensen goes down”.
“100% in agreement,” replied Jason Calacanis, a host of the “All-In” podcast, which is a popular podcast hosted by a group of venture capitalists including David Sacks, President Donald Trump’s former AI and crypto czar.
Antonio Gracias, founder of Valor Equity Partners and a long-time associate of Musk, agreed on Nov 10: “America would not be ahead in the AI race without Jensen. He clearly made a mistake. One mistake does not erase a lifetime of leadership.”
The “All-In” hosts have been close to Huang. During an appearance onstage with the podcast’s hosts in September, Huang took a phone call from Trump.
Trump, too, has stood by Huang.
“I really believe him,” he said on Nov 9, recalling a conversation when Huang told him he did not know that Alice Huang was a spy. The New York Times has reported that Trump was briefed a year ago about intelligence showing that she was an operative for the Chinese government. Trump on Nov 10 demurred when asked whether he received the briefing in 2025.
Huang has been among Washington’s most forceful voices against cutting China off from American chips, and has been an ally of Trump since his return to office.
[truncated]

A498.text:
Jensen Huang said to have had relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, who reports to him
Ryan Mac, Tripp Mickle and Georgia Gee
- Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief, is under scrutiny over an affair with a woman alleged by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy, while Nvidia has opened a board investigation.
- Five former Nvidia workers said Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, a vice president who reports to him, and their conduct may breach company rules.
- The pair were seen being affectionate at a March conference hotel, and Huang’s security allegedly tried to contain a bystander and seek a nondisclosure agreement.
AI generated
Jensen Huang, the leader of Nvidia who is under investigation for an affair with a woman whom US intelligence determined is a Chinese spy, also had an extramarital relationship with an executive who reports to him, according to five people who worked at the company.
The relationship, which has not been previously reported, was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, said the people, who spoke under the condition of anonymity to describe sensitive information. 
Under Nvidia’s code of conduct, employees are told to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships”, and the company states that it “promptly investigates reports of misconduct”.
Many corporations have policies against managers having relationships with subordinates.
Huang, 63, and Powell, 48, were captured on video being affectionate at a San Jose, California, hotel during an Nvidia conference in March, according to two of the people who worked at the company. The New York Times has not seen the video.
Both Huang and Powell are married to other people.
Huang, who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has turned it into the premier supplier of artificial intelligence chips, has been under intensifying scrutiny. In October, The New York Times reported that a Chinese executive he had become close to had been identified by US officials as a Chinese intelligence asset.
In November, after Huang acknowledged the affair, Nvidia’s board opened an investigation into the matter that is being led by the law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. The Republican leaders of three influential House committees have also asked Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with the woman, who goes by the name Alice Huang.
China has denied the espionage claims. Alice Huang, the Chinese executive accused of spying for Beijing, has not responded to requests for comment.
When reached by phone on Nov 11 and asked about his relationship with Powell, Jensen Huang said: “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up.
Nvidia declined to provide a statement. Powell did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company’s shares fell about 8% in after-hours trading.
Kimberly Powell has risen through Nvidia’s ranks
Jensen Huang’s relationship with Powell has been discussed inside the company, the five people said.
Powell joined Nvidia in 2008. She oversees programmes that could apply Nvidia’s chip technology to higher education and healthcare, particularly medical imaging devices, according to the company’s website.
Powell has risen through Nvidia’s ranks. She was promoted to senior director of AI business development in 2016, according to her LinkedIn profile. By late 2017, she had been appointed vice-president of healthcare. She attends technology conferences around the world, and delivers speeches on behalf of the company.
In March, Powell appeared at GTC, Nvidia’s annual developer conference in San Jose, where she spoke about using AI to aid in breakthroughs in healthcare and biology. Her presentation used cartoon depictions of Jensen Huang.
During the conference, Nvidia executives were at a nearby hotel for meetings. 
Huang and Powell were seen being affectionate at the hotel.
[truncated]

A499.text:
Nvidia board meets to decide CEO Huang’s future as leadership crisis deepens
Nvidia’s board is meeting late on Nov 11 to decide whether to oust chief executive Jensen Huang, a source familiar with the matter told Reuters, as the world’s dominant supplier of AI chips grapples with reports of two extramarital affairs involving its long-time leader.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the board meeting.
The meeting marks a sharp shift from Nov 8, when Nvidia’s board expressed confidence in Huang and his leadership team.
Under Nvidia’s by-laws, Huang can be removed “with or without cause” by a majority vote of directors.
Nvidia has 11 directors and considers all but Huang independent.
Nvidia’s stock slid around 7% in early Frankfurt trading on Nov 12 after the Wall Street Journal first reported that the company was preparing to fire Huang.
If those losses hold, Nvidia will have lost about US$600 billion (S$770.5 billion) in market value since the board announced its investigation into his relationship with a businesswoman called Alice Huang alleged to be a Chinese spy.
Revelations that US intelligence was probing Alice Huang for facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms set off a series of events: Wall Street began raising questions about Nvidia’s governance and Jensen Huang’s personal conduct, while the company’s board launched an internal investigation and hired outside counsel.
Lawmakers also began to push for tighter curbs on chip exports to China.
China has denied the allegations. Reuters was not able to contact Alice Huang for comment.
“The market is starting to price Nvidia without its founder as the likely outcome, not a tail risk,” said Armina Rosenberg, portfolio manager and co-founder of Minotaur Capital, which holds Nvidia shares. “Losing Jensen would be a real blow.”
Bernstein and Oppenheimer both downgraded Nvidia following the latest developments and Citi cut its target.
“A leadership transition creates an overhang on the stock given his central role in strategy, product vision, customer relationships, and investor confidence,” Citi analysts wrote.
No obvious successor
Huang’s potential departure would leave a leadership vacuum at the roughly US$4 trillion chipmaker he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the dominant supplier of AI chips at the centre of the global artificial-intelligence boom and US-China technology rivalry.
Huang, 63, has no obvious successor and owns about 3.6% of Nvidia’s stock. He also has dozens of direct reports, underscoring the tight control he maintains over the company.
Bloomberg reported on Nov 11 that Nvidia’s board has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Huang, citing a source familiar with the situation.
Rosenberg said chief financial officer Colette Kress, who has held the role for more than a decade, would be the natural choice as an interim CEO, but said the bigger question was who would lead Nvidia’s technology roadmap longer term.
Odds on prediction market website Polymarket shifted sharply to show an 88% chance that Huang would resign or be removed by the end of the year.
Odds for his successor favoured Ian Buck, who oversees the business that serves Nvidia’s data centre clients.
The leadership turmoil comes just days before investors are set to hear from the company on its financial performance and outlook, with its quarterly results due on Nov 17.
Earlier in the day, the New York Times reported that Huang had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.
The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five sources who worked at the company.
When reached by phone on Nov 11 and asked about his relationship with Powell, Huang said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly.” He then hung up, the New York Times reported.
[truncated]

A508.text:
Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones; Iran-aligned group denies targeting Mecca
DUBAI – Saudi air defences intercepted Houthi missiles and drones launched towards Riyadh, Mecca and other regions on Nov 11, as hostilities between the Iran-aligned group and the kingdom worsen.
The Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Yemeni group said it had intercepted and destroyed three cruise missiles headed to the Riyadh region, two drones aimed at Mecca and southern areas and two missiles pointed towards the west.
Mecca, home to sites sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam’s holiest city and the focal point of the annual haj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims undertake each year.
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree later denied targeting Mecca with a drone, saying the group’s operations target oil facilities and military bases.
Saree also said the Houthis had attacked a pumping station in Saudi Arabia’s Yanbu, a key Saudi oil hub that allows exports to avoid the blocked Strait of Hormuz. There was no Saudi confirmation of the Houthi statement.
Saudi civil defence issued alerts warning of potential danger in the cities of Taif, Yanbu and Khamis Mushait later on Nov 11, then announced the danger had passed, state television reported.
The militia, which controls most of the populous parts of Yemen, has intensified attacks on the Saudi capital, in recent days, saying it was responding to Saudi attacks in Yemen. A Houthi attack on Nov 8 damaged an Aramco administrative building in Riyadh’s financial hub.
The Nov 11 interceptions marked the second consecutive day that Saudi air defences had intercepted Houthi missiles launched towards Riyadh, after they downed a ballistic missile and a cruise missile on Nov 10, the coalition said.
In October, a Houthi attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
Renewed fighting between the two sides has intensified since September, when the Houthis advanced towards the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis have since stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up air strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response. REUTERS

A527.text:
Ukraine faces 'systemic speed restrictions' on Starshield again that 'help Russians kill more Ukrainians', Zelenskyy says
Oh-oh.
Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy has just taken to X to say that the Ukrainian army is once again experiencing “significant disruptions to Starshield’s operations over the territory of Ukraine.”
He said the problem has been going on “for several days now,” affecting operations “along the entire frontline and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.”
“Specifically, systematic speed restrictions are being imposed on Starshield, limiting it to 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions.”
Spelling out the real life consequences, Zelenskyy said the disruption complicates intercepting Russian jet-powered drones, with “strikes that got through because our interception systems cannot reach sufficient speeds and are unable to intercept in time.”
“Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine. We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side.”
Heightened security measures in Dublin with 'largest deployment in history'
Ireland’s Martin was also asked about any potential bomb threats or any other potential disruptions to the summit.
He said that the Irish police “are best placed to make judgment calls in respect of this,” and “have established protocols” in place to deal with any issue.
Irish public broadcaster RTÉ reported that some 5,000 police officers will be on the streets of Dublin, “the largest deployment … in the history of the force in an operation that has been described as unique and complex.”
EU needs a 'clear, coherent' leadership voice in Ukraine talks, Ireland's Martin says
Meanwhile, over in Dublin, Ireland’s Micheál Martin has stressed the need to have a “clear, coherent” European voice in the Ukraine talks, as he answered reporters’ questions ahead of today’s meeting of the European Political Community in Dublin.
He said that the issue of Europe’s representation in any talks on Ukraine will be discussed “in the margins” today, with a more formal discussion at the EU informal summit tomorrow.
He said there were “some obvious candidates” as to who could represent the EU, but declined to speculate on names, other than stressing “there is clearly a need for a coherent voice agreed by the EU27.”
Curiously, he said the EU voice around the table “is not necessarily one person,” but “a clear, coherent leadership” voice from the EU.
“Obviously, Europe will want a voice at that table, particularly in so far as issued impact on Europe, because of the economic inputs, the security inputs, and in terms of Ukraine’s membership of the EU.”
He also defended the EU’s involvement so far, saying the coalition of the willing “has been particularly impactful” in “persuading the US on quite a number of issues.”
Martin also said Europe continues to be “genuinely shocked at the level of death and destruction” coming from Russia’s actions in Ukraine and “the imperialist agenda of Vladimir Putin.”
On the Abu Dhabi talks, Martin welcomed the potential prisoners swap as a “significant measure in and of itself,” welcoming the work of Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on these issues ahead of their arrival to Dublin later tonight.
“I think the objective of tonight’s meeting is to debrief president Zelenskyy on the engagement by Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with president Putin, and it’s a moving situation.
Our view up to now has been that Russia hasn’t shown any genuine interest in a peaceful resolution of this conflict.

A561.text:
Senior Iranian officials believe the US is planning either further military strikes or an ever-tightening economic stranglehold that will push Tehran into retaliatory action.
The assessment comes from Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Iran’s chief negotiator in talks with the US, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.
Mohammadi said on his Telegram channel that the Americans had proposed a timeframe of about two weeks after which Donald Trump would make a decision on military action. Mohammadi, who is regarded as a reliable indicator of Ghalibaf’s thinking, cast doubt on the US president’s claim that the military option was off the table. He claimed Washington was preparing for a limited strike and Iran was already preparing a response.
If the US sanctions continued, he said, a comprehensive pre-emptive war would be needed “to increase the cost of sanctions for the enemy”.
Mohammadi described the US response to Iran’s latest proposals on reopening the strait of Hormuz as “not only unsatisfactory but completely deceptive”. “They do not want to release the frozen funds,” he said. “They do not want to lift the sanctions and they do not want to stop the war in Lebanon.”
He also disclosed that Iran had rejected a request from the US vice-president, JD Vance, for a direct meeting with its negotiators before giving a response to Tehran’s conditions for lifting the siege on the strait.
For now, Trump has settled on a strategy of suffocating Iran through economic pressure and tightening the blockade on its oil exports while facilitating those of other Gulf states through Hormuz.
Mohammadi’s assessments suggest some senior Iranians fear Washington’s strategy might work by destabilising the country. The thinking goes that economic turmoil might spark street protests, potentially around the anniversary of nationwide demonstrations that began in late December last year.
On this basis, the Iranian leadership might conclude that the status quo – a “no peace, no war” impasse – was not sustainable and pre-emptive action was required.
Despite Iranian claims that their blockade of the strait is working, there is concern that Brent crude is at a relatively low $93 a barrel, while Saudi oil production is near prewar levels of 9.3m barrels a day. In an attempt to close any loopholes, Iran said it bombed a US radar post on the Omani island of Didamar three days ago.
In another development, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s national security council, said he had told Russia that Iran was not prepared for even a particle of its highly enriched stockpile of uranium to leave the country, saying it might be needed for planned nuclear-powered submarines.
A third senior official, Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Mojtaba Khamenei, Iran’s supreme leader, warned Europe that any complicity in the US blockade would be “an act of war that will be etched in the nation’s historical memory”.
Tehran has been increasingly clear that US bases in Europe will be targeted if fighting resumes. Rezaei said: “If American planes take off from a distant military base and come to this country to bomb Iran, we will also target that base. We are announcing this now so they have no excuse tomorrow.”
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, gave the impression this week that the policy of economic strangulation was sufficient and described Iran’s demands as unrealistic. However, Trump is under pressure to resolve the crisis before the Democrats take charge of Congress on 3 January.
A Reuters Ipsos poll in the US shows 71% of Americans want Congress to pass legislation to end the war in Iran. The overwhelming message from the midterm elections was that the conflict was highly unpopular but the Democrats do not have a strategy to end it and open up the strait of Hormuz. This risks leaving the political initiative with the White House, and an increasingly hardline Iranian leadership.
